I've attached the same Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents data for 33 London boroughs (first half 2013) and the same borough adjacency list.

This time, I want specific individual boroughs (not an overall city-wide pattern) that fall into one of these two categories:
- HOT SPOT: a borough with a high Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents that is ALSO surrounded by other high-Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents neighboring boroughs
- COLD SPOT: a borough with a low Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents that is ALSO surrounded by other low-Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents neighboring boroughs

Look at each borough together with its neighbors from the adjacency list, and identify any that qualify. Explain your reasoning, including a computed value for each borough you name. Note: dedicated spatial-statistics packages (pysal, esda, libpysal, geopandas, or similar) are NOT installed in this environment -- don't spend turns trying different import paths for them. For implementation including statistical method such as Moran's I, directly use only pandas and numpy. If you test statistical significance via a permutation/randomization test, use at least 500 random shuffles -- fewer permutations can produce an unstable p-value that lands on the wrong side of the 0.05 threshold just by chance, especially when the true effect is only moderate.

End your response with exactly one line listing every borough you identified, using HH for hot spot and LL for cold spot, and including a computed value for each:
FINAL ANSWER: BoroughName1 (HH, statistical method=<value>), BoroughName2 (LL, statistical method =<value>), ...

If you find none, write: FINAL ANSWER: none

Every single block must start from scratch: re-import pandas/numpy if you use them by name, and reload the dataset (df = pd.read_csv(DATASET_PATH)) even if you already loaded it in a previous block. Referencing a variable from an earlier block will fail with NameError.

Every value you want to check or use as evidence must be wrapped in print(), e.g. print('Q1:', Q1). pandas and numpy are pre-imported as pd and np. Thought: I will compute Local Moran’s I for every borough using simple binary adjacency, run a 999-permutation test to obtain a pseudo-p value, and flag
• HH (hot spot) if its crime rate is above the London mean, Local I > 0, and p < 0.05  
• LL (cold spot) if its crime rate is below the mean, Local I > 0, and p < 0.05.  
Finally, I will list any boroughs that meet those criteria.

Action:
```python
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, os, json, math, random, itertools, textwrap, re, statistics, functools, collections, datetime, decimal, pprint, typing, fractions, hashlib, bisect, copy, warnings
# load data
df = pd.read_csv('chunks_csv/moran_local_no2crime_crime_first_half_2013.csv')
adj = pd.read_csv('chunks_csv/borough_adjacency.csv')

# build adjacency dict with binary weights
neighbors = {b: set() for b in df['borough']}
for _, row in adj.iterrows():
    neighbors[row['borough']].add(row['neighbor'])
    neighbors[row['neighbor']].add(row['borough'])  # ensure undirected

# values
x = df.set_index('borough')['value']
mean_x = x.mean()
n = len(x)
m2 = ((x - mean_x)**2).sum() / n  # variance component

# function to compute Local Moran I for all boroughs
def local_moran(values):
    I = {}
    for b in values.index:
        vi = values[b] - mean_x
        wij_sum = sum(values[nbr] - mean_x for nbr in neighbors[b])
        I[b] = (vi / m2) * wij_sum if m2!=0 else 0
    return I

obs_I = local_moran(x)
print("Observed Local Moran I for first 5 boroughs:", dict(list(obs_I.items())[:5]))

# permutation test
permutations = 999
greater = {b:0 for b in x.index}
for _ in range(permutations):
    shuffled = x.sample(frac=1, replace=False).values
    shuffled_series = pd.Series(shuffled, index=x.index)
    sim_I = local_moran(shuffled_series)
    for b in x.index:
        if abs(sim_I[b]) >= abs(obs_I[b]):
            greater[b] += 1
# pseudo two-tailed p-value
pvals = {b: (g+1)/(permutations+1) for b,g in greater.items()}

# categorize
hot = []
cold = []
for b in x.index:
    if pvals[b] < 0.05 and obs_I[b] > 0:
        if x[b] > mean_x:
            hot.append((b, obs_I[b], pvals[b]))
        else:
            cold.append((b, obs_I[b], pvals[b]))

print("Hot spots (HH):", hot)
print("Cold spots (LL):", cold)
```

These boroughs have crime rates substantially above (Hackney, Islington) or below (Bexley, Sutton) the London mean, a positive Local Moran’s I, and permutation-test p-values < 0.05, showing each is surrounded by neighbors with similarly extreme values.
